prompt: In a versioned bucket, `aws s3 rm s3://bucket/key` runs with no version id. What is in the bucket afterwards?
hint: A delete with no version adds something.

choices.text: Nothing under that key: the latest version was removed and the older ones with it
choices.why: Nothing was removed; that is the point of versioning.

choices.text: Every version it had, under a new delete marker
choices.why: Right. The marker makes the key answer `NoSuchKey`, and deleting the marker brings it back.

choices.text: The older versions, and the latest moved to a recycle prefix
choices.why: S3 has no recycle prefix; the latest version stays where it was, under the marker.

choices.text: Only the latest version, marked noncurrent
choices.why: The older versions stay too; every version is kept.

prompt: A script deleted `customers/customers.csv` in a versioned bucket. What brings the file back with its last contents?
hint: What did the script add?

choices.text: Uploading the file again from a backup
choices.why: That works if a backup exists, and adds a third version; the bytes were never gone.

choices.text: Deleting the delete marker
choices.why: Right. Removing the marker makes the last real version the latest again.

choices.text: `restore-object`, as for an archived object
choices.why: A restore is for Glacier classes and is refused for anything else.

choices.text: Suspending versioning, which undoes the last delete
choices.why: Suspending changes how new writes are versioned and undoes nothing.

prompt: Put the versioning states of a bucket in the order a bucket can pass through them, from its creation.
hint: There is no way back to the first.

prompt: In moto, after suspending versioning and writing the key once more, an older version id answers `NoSuchVersion`. What does that tell you about S3?
hint: Is moto the reference for what S3 keeps?

choices.text: That moto is wrong here: S3 keeps the old versions
choices.why: Right. And it fails in the dangerous direction, making a cleanup look done that was not.

choices.text: That suspending versioning is a cheap, safe way to get rid of every old version
choices.why: On S3 they stay, listed and billed; removing them takes a delete per version or a rule.

choices.text: That S3 keeps old versions only for 24 hours after a suspension
choices.why: There is no such window; they stay until deleted.

choices.text: That the `null` version is a copy of all the earlier ones
choices.why: It holds one write, the latest.

prompt: A versioned bucket holds one 50 GB table rewritten every night, and `aws s3 ls` shows 50 GB. Why is that the wrong number for the bill?
hint: What does a listing show, and what is billed?

choices.text: `aws s3 ls` rounds sizes down to the nearest 50 GB
choices.why: It prints bytes exactly; it just prints only the current versions.

choices.text: Versions are billed at Standard-IA, so the listing overstates the bill
choices.why: A noncurrent version is billed in its own class, the same as the current one here.

choices.text: Only the current version is listed; old ones are billed too
choices.why: Right. After 360 nights with no rule that is 18,000 GB billed for a 50 GB table.

choices.text: Delete markers are billed as full copies
choices.why: A marker has no bytes; the cost is in the versions.

prompt: A 20 GB table is rewritten every night in a versioned bucket, with a rule expiring noncurrent versions 7 days after they are replaced. Once the rule has settled, how many GB does the bucket hold for it?
hint: The current version plus the ones replaced in the last seven days.

prompt: A table is read once a month, at the month's close. How long should its noncurrent versions live, and why?
hint: A version is useful while somebody would still notice the bad write.

choices.text: Seven days, the right number for any table
choices.why: Seven fits a table read daily; a broken write here may go unseen for weeks.

choices.text: A month and a few days
choices.why: Right. A bad write is still recoverable when it is noticed at the close; the number is how long a mistake can go unnoticed.

choices.text: Forever, since versions cost nothing
choices.why: Each one is billed in full; a year with no rule was over twenty times the cost.

choices.text: One day, to keep the bill lowest
choices.why: Cheapest, and a bad write found at the month's close would have no way back.

prompt: A rule moves objects under `now/` to Glacier after 0 days. In moto, `head-object` on a new object there still shows Standard. Why?
hint: What in moto would apply the rule?

choices.text: The object is under 128 KB, so the rule skips it
choices.why: It was 200,000 bytes, above that line.

choices.text: Rules apply only to objects written before the rule existed
choices.why: Rules apply to every object their filter matches.

choices.text: moto stores rules and never applies them; nothing in it ages
choices.why: Right. On AWS the next daily run would move it.

choices.text: A transition needs at least 30 days
choices.why: That minimum is for Standard-IA and One Zone-IA, not Glacier.

prompt: Match each problem to the life-cycle action that solves it.
hint: Two of them are about versions.

pairs.left: Exports older than a year are read only for audits
Replaced versions of a nightly table pile up
Parts of uploads that died halfway are billed
Scratch files must be gone after a week

prompt: moto accepted a rule moving objects to Standard-IA after 10 days. What does S3 do with the same rule?
hint: There is a minimum time in Standard before that class.

choices.text: Accepts it and waits 30 days anyway
choices.why: S3 does not correct a rule; it refuses it.

choices.text: Accepts it, since moto and S3 check rules the same way
choices.why: moto checks less than S3, which is why the rule files are checked by you.

choices.text: Accepts it and charges the remaining 20 days as early deletion
choices.why: Early deletion is about leaving a class early; this rule never gets written.

choices.text: Refuses it: the days must be at least 30
choices.why: Right. moto only confirmed that the file parses.

prompt: By default since 2024, a life-cycle rule does not transition objects smaller than ___ KB.
hint: `TransitionDefaultMinimumObjectSize` names it.

prompt: An invoice version is locked in compliance mode. `delete-object` without a version id succeeds. Was the invoice destroyed?
hint: A lock protects versions, not keys.

choices.text: Yes: moto let it through because it evaluates no policy
choices.why: S3 would let it through as well; the delete only adds a marker.

choices.text: No: a marker now hides it, and it survives underneath
choices.why: Right. The key can be hidden; the version cannot be destroyed.

choices.text: Yes, after the next life-cycle run
choices.why: A rule cannot remove a locked version before its date either.

choices.text: No, because a locked key refuses every delete
choices.why: The delete without a version succeeded; it is the version that is locked.

prompt: Quitanda wants a small break-glass role able to remove a locked version in an emergency, and nobody else. Which setup does that on AWS?
hint: One mode has a bypass, and the bypass is a permission.

choices.text: Compliance mode, with root as the break-glass identity
choices.why: Not even root can remove a compliance-locked version before its date.

choices.text: A legal hold on every version, switched off by the role
choices.why: Anyone allowed `s3:PutObjectLegalHold` can switch it off, and a hold is meant for an unknown end date, not as a permission scheme.

choices.text: Governance mode, with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` allowed only to that role
choices.why: Right. The bypass works only for an identity whose policy allows it.

choices.text: Versioning with MFA delete
choices.why: That ties deletes to the root user's device, not to a role.

prompt: A version has a governance retention that ended yesterday and a legal hold that is on. A delete is sent with `--bypass-governance-retention`. What happens?
hint: The hold has no date and no bypass.

choices.text: It is refused: the hold blocks the delete until it is switched off
choices.why: Right. Governance's bypass does not reach a legal hold.

choices.text: It succeeds, since the retention has ended
choices.why: The retention has ended, and the hold is a separate lock.

choices.text: It succeeds, since the bypass overrides every kind of lock a version can carry
choices.why: It overrides governance retention and nothing else.

choices.text: It adds a delete marker and leaves the version
choices.why: A delete naming a version adds no marker; this one is simply refused.

prompt: When can Object Lock be turned on for a bucket, according to the section?
hint: Look at the command that made the archive bucket.

choices.text: At any time, with `put-object-lock-configuration` on the bucket
choices.why: That call sets a default on a bucket that already has the lock; it is enabled at creation.

choices.text: When the bucket is created, which turns versioning on too
choices.why: Right. That is why it was `s3api create-bucket` with `--object-lock-enabled-for-bucket`.

choices.text: After the first object is written, when the bucket has a version to lock
choices.why: Writing objects has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: With `aws s3 mb --lock`
choices.why: `aws s3 mb` has no such option.

prompt: In moto, a compliance retention was changed to governance and the version deleted. What can a test against moto prove about a lock?
hint: Shape, or strength?

choices.text: That compliance mode can be undone by an administrator
choices.why: On S3 it cannot, by anybody, the root user included.

choices.text: Nothing at all, so moto is useless for locks
choices.why: It shows the requests are well formed and the plain delete is refused.

choices.text: That the requests are well formed, and no more
choices.why: Right. Test the shape against moto and believe AWS's documentation for the strength.

choices.text: That the lock holds, since moto refused the first delete
choices.why: It refused that one and then allowed the retention to be shortened.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer governance mode with a bypass role over MFA delete?
hint: Who holds the device, and what else stops working?

choices.text: MFA delete ties every permanent delete to the root user's device, and rules out life-cycle configuration
choices.why: Right. One device in one person's hand, and no rule to expire noncurrent versions.

choices.text: MFA delete costs extra per request
choices.why: The lesson names no price for it; the objection is who holds the device.

choices.text: MFA delete works only in us-east-1
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson ties it to a region.

choices.text: MFA delete can be turned on from the console by anyone
choices.why: Only root can turn it on, and never from the console.

prompt: Quitanda's invoices must survive a person with stolen administrator keys for five years. Which of these are part of that on AWS? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which protections can an administrator not undo?

choices.text: A bucket created with Object Lock
choices.why: Yes: the lock can only be enabled at creation.

choices.text: A default retention in compliance mode of five years
choices.why: Yes: nobody can shorten or lift it.

choices.text: Versioning alone
choices.why: Whoever may delete a marker may delete the versions too.

choices.text: Governance mode, with the bypass allowed to administrators
choices.why: The stolen keys are an administrator's, so the bypass is theirs too.

prompt: Order the life of an export under Quitanda's `orders-age-out` rule.
A 10 GB file is overwritten every night for 30 nights in a versioned bucket with no rule. On the 30th night, how many GB does the bucket hold for that key?
hint: Every write is a version, and none expires.
